why: The measurement that opened the rule: a repository with four credentials of real shape -- an AWS access key, a GitHub token, an LLM API key and a literal assigned to `apiKey` -- came out of `rebar-security .` as "2 of 2, 1 not applicable, EXIT 0" and out of `rebar .` with none of the 23 rules mentioning a credential, while `tooling/secret/scan-secret.mjs` exited 1 with all four on the same tree. The detector existed and was a rule of no ruler: it ran only in the pre-commit hook, which is N5 and disappears with `git commit --no-verify` leaving no diff. The fail side is that tree. The pass side carries six NAMED false positives, and each one locks a different piece of the scanner's defense: the documentation line that quotes a vendor prefix (the single false positive in 44 attack cases), a value that comes from `process.env`, a `key` with no qualifier, a connection string to localhost, the written `rebar-segredo-ok:` escape, and the `.env.example` placeholder in the unquoted form. Whoever makes this rule read the code WITHOUT comments -- and the temptation is real, because every other rule in this module reads that way -- kills the escape hatch already written into the audited repositories and the pass side goes red. Whoever drops the proof-root filter keeps both sides green and turns rebar's own 345 case files into an accusation, which is why `security-self` is the other half of this proof.
